title: Slice a big hailstone in half and you find rings inside, like an onion
body: A hailstone begins as a water droplet in a thunderstorm, carried upward by updrafts that can blow at up to **180 km/h**. Above the freezing level, droplets stay liquid even below 0 °C, and they freeze onto the rising stone. Where droplets are plentiful it gains a thick layer of clear ice; where there is mostly water vapour, a thin layer of white ice full of tiny air bubbles. Passing through zones like these on the way up builds the rings, and newer research says a single trip through the storm can be enough.

cover.alt: A huge lumpy white hailstone lying on a towel next to a tape measure

slides.question: How wide was the largest hailstone ever officially measured?
slides.explanation: About 20 cm (7.9 in) across, with a circumference of 47.3 cm. It fell at Vivian, South Dakota, on 23 July 2010, and it is the stone on the cover.

slides.alt: Animation: a hailstone is sliced to show clear and white rings. In a diagram of a storm cloud, a droplet rides the updraft above the freezing level and rises through bands of droplets and vapour, gaining a clear or a white layer in each; an old up-and-down path is struck out, and the stone falls.
slides.music: “Stay the Course” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.alt: A hailstone cut in half on a wooden board, showing rings of clear and milky white ice around a white core
slides.caption: A real hailstone cut open. Each ring is a layer of ice it picked up on its way through the storm cloud.

slides.heading: How many trips does it take?

left.label: Old idea
left.text: A hailstone falls and is carried up again many times, adding a layer on each trip through the cloud.

right.label: Newer research
right.text: One trip through zones with more or less supercooled water can build the layers. Repeated trips aren’t needed to explain them.

slides.heading: How fast hailstones fall
slides.note: Estimates: real speeds vary with shape, wind, collisions and melting

slides.label: the heaviest hailstone on record
slides.text: It fell in Gopalganj District, Bangladesh, on 14 April 1986.

slides.question: What makes a hailstone’s white layers cloudy instead of clear?
slides.explanation: White ice freezes fast and traps small air bubbles, which make it opaque. When the stone grows wetter, the bubbles join up and escape, so that ice is clear.
